nameStory: The 'clove pink' gets its name from its distinctive spicy fragrance that smells remarkably like the cloves you might find in your kitchen spice rack. This delightful scent is actually a combination of cinnamon and nutmeg aromas, making it one of the most pleasantly fragrant flowers you'll encounter. The name 'carnation' comes from the Latin word for flesh, referring to the pink color of the original wild flowers.
description: Clove pink, better known as carnation, is a Mediterranean native that occasionally shows up in New England gardens and rarely escapes to the wild. This fragrant flowering plant produces distinctive ruffled blooms with deeply fringed petals that look like they've been cut with pinking shears. The flowers sit atop slender stems that can reach 1-2 feet tall, rising from narrow, blue-green leaves. While carnations come in many colors through cultivation, wild types are typically pink to white.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five deeply fringed petals create a ruffled, almost shredded appearance around the flower's edge. The blooms emit a strong, sweet, spicy fragrance reminiscent of cloves or cinnamon when you lean in close.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, linear leaves are blue-green to gray-green in color and grow in opposite pairs along the stem. They feel somewhat thick and waxy to the touch, with a smooth texture and prominent parallel veins.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms compact clumps or mats of foliage with flower stems rising 12-24 inches above the base. The plant has a somewhat sprawling, cushion-like growth pattern typical of Mediterranean plants.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flower stems are smooth, pale green, and noticeably swollen at the joints where leaves attach. The stems feel firm and somewhat succulent when gently squeezed.

habitat: In New England, clove pink is extremely rare in the wild, with only one recorded observation. When found, it's typically in disturbed areas near old gardens, along roadsides, or in sunny, well-drained spots where garden plants might escape cultivation. It prefers alkaline soils and full sun, struggling in New England's typically acidic, moist conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as blue-green tufts of narrow leaves. Plants begin developing flower buds in late spring as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in early to mid-summer, when the intensely fragrant flowers are most abundant and the spicy clove scent is strongest on warm days.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue sporadically into early fall. The evergreen foliage remains blue-green and provides the best identification feature as blooms fade.
seasonality.winter: In mild winters, the narrow leaves may persist as low evergreen tufts, though plants often don't survive New England's harsh conditions.

funFact: Carnations have been cultivated for over 2,000 years, making them one of humanity's oldest garden flowers - so old that botanists can't even pinpoint where the original wild plants naturally grew because they've been moved around and hybridized for millennia!
confusionNotes: The deeply fringed petals are unique among New England flowers, but other Dianthus species (pinks) share the opposite leaves and swollen stem joints. Remember: if it smells strongly of spices and has dramatically ruffled petal edges, it's likely clove pink rather than its smaller, less fragrant relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'pink,' carnations come in many colors - the word 'pink' actually comes from the flower, not the color! The pink color was named after these flowers because of their characteristic fringed edges that look 'pinked' (cut in a zigzag pattern). Most carnations in New England are garden escapes rather than truly naturalized plants.
compareHints: Clove pink differs from other New England Dianthus species by its much larger size, intensely fragrant flowers, and dramatically fringed petals. Deptford pink and maiden pink are much smaller with less fragrant, less ruffled flowers. Sweet William has clustered flowers rather than single blooms, and Cheddar pink forms tighter mats with smaller, less fragrant flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its showier relatives like Sweet William or garden carnations, Deptford pink is much smaller and more delicate with white to very pale pink flowers rather than bright colors.
Maiden pink differs from its Dianthus relatives by its smaller size and grass-like growth habit.
Unlike its cousin Deptford pink which has tiny, sparse flowers and grows as a weedy annual, Sweet William produces large, dense flower clusters and grows much taller.
Cheddar pink differs from its Dianthus cousins by its extremely compact, cushion-forming habit and intensely fragrant flowers.
